section.title: Practical Warnings
section.sectionRationale: A cluster of four short, practical warnings breaks from the sustained argument style of the surrounding discourses: reckless financial pledges, verses 1 to 5, laziness taught by the ant, verses 6 to 11, the troublemaker who sows discord, verses 12 to 15, and a numbered list of what the LORD hates, verses 16 to 19, closing the section with a clear moral summary.
section.thesis: Wisdom is intensely practical, it warns against foolish financial entanglements, exposes the sluggard's self deception, names the scheming troublemaker for what he is, and finally lists, in the LORD's own reckoning, the very things His heart detests.
section.frameNote: Four short movements: escaping a reckless pledge of security, verses 1 to 5; a lesson in diligence from the ant, verses 6 to 11; the portrait of a worthless, discord sowing man, verses 12 to 15; and the seven things the LORD hates, verses 16 to 19.

verses.text: My son, if you have put up security for your neighbor, if you have struck hands in pledge with a stranger,
if you have been trapped by the words of your lips, ensnared by the words of your mouth,
then do this, my son, to free yourself, for you have fallen into your neighbor's hands: Go, humble yourself, and press your plea with your neighbor.
Allow no sleep to your eyes or slumber to your eyelids.
Free yourself, like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the snare of the fowler.
Walk in the manner of the ant, O {{atsel|slacker}}; observe its ways and become wise.
Without a commander, without an overseer or ruler,
it prepares its provisions in summer; it gathers its food at harvest.
How long will you lie there, O slacker? When will you get up from your sleep?
A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest,
and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit.
A {{beliyaal|worthless person}}, a wicked man, walks with a perverse mouth,
winking his eyes, speaking with his feet, and pointing with his fingers.
With deceit in his heart he devises evil; he continually sows discord.
Therefore calamity will come upon him suddenly; in an instant he will be shattered beyond recovery.
There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are {{toebah|detestable}} to Him:
haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood,
a heart that devises wicked schemes, feet that run swiftly to evil,
a false witness who gives false testimony, and one who stirs up discord among brothers.

atsel.gloss: The sluggard or slacker, a recurring character throughout Proverbs. Here he is sent to school by an insect, the ant, whose diligence without any external commander exposes the sluggard's self chosen, self deceiving idleness for what it is.

beliyaal.gloss: A worthless person, literally one without value or profit, a term that became a name for wickedness itself, Belial, later used of Satan, 2 Corinthians 6:15. Here he schemes with body language, winking, pointing, before his sudden, irrecoverable downfall.

toebah.gloss: Detestable or abominable, a strong term for what is morally repugnant to God, used elsewhere of idolatry and covenant breaking. The list in verses 17 to 19 shows that God's hatred is not reserved for religious offenses alone but extends to pride, dishonesty, violence, and division among His people.

basic.context: This short section gathers four separate, very practical warnings. First, if you have rashly guaranteed someone else's debt, get out of it urgently and humbly. Second, if you are lazy, learn diligence from an ant, who needs no boss to keep working. Third, beware the schemer who plots evil with sly body language and sows discord, whose sudden downfall cannot be undone. Finally, the section climaxes with a list, in God's own words, of seven things He detests, pride, lying, violence, scheming, eagerness for evil, false testimony, and stirring up discord.
basic.hermeneutics: Each warning stands on its own as concrete, situational wisdom rather than abstract theology, yet together they build toward the numbered list in verses 16 to 19, which functions as a summarizing moral compass for the whole cluster. The 'six, even seven' numbering is a common Hebrew poetic device for completeness, not a claim that only exactly seven things offend God.
basic.originalLanguages: The atsel, sluggard, is shamed by the ant's self motivated diligence, verse 6, a vivid picture used because insects were assumed to lack the reasoning capacity humans have no excuse to squander. The beliyyaal, worthless person, of verse 12 carries a weight beyond mere laziness or foolishness, it became a name for embodied wickedness, later even a title for Satan. And the list closes on things toebah, detestable, to the LORD, a strong covenantal word usually reserved for idolatry, now applied to pride, violence, and discord among God's people.
basic.typology: The false witness and the sower of discord, verse 19, anticipate the very charges brought against Christ at His trial, false witnesses testifying against Him, Matthew 26:59 to 60, so that the very sins this passage names God as hating were, in a supreme irony, used to condemn the innocent Son of God.
basic.christ: This list of things the LORD hates, haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, false testimony, discord among brothers, describes exactly the conspiracy that convicted Jesus, false witnesses were sought against Him, Matthew 26:59 to 60, and His innocent blood was shed by proud and scheming men. Christ bore the very sins this passage condemns, absorbing their worst expression at the cross, so that He might forgive both those who commit them and those who suffer under them.
basic.god: God's hatred here is not arbitrary, it targets pride, deceit, violence, scheming, eagerness for evil, false testimony, and division, each one an assault on the truth, on human life, or on community. This same God is patient with the sluggard and the reckless debtor, offering practical ways back rather than instant condemnation, showing that His hatred of sin coexists with real patience toward the sinner who still has time to change course.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 26:59 to 60 shows false witnesses sought against Jesus, echoing verse 19. Romans 12:18 calls believers to live at peace with everyone, opposing the discord of verse 19. James 4:6 opposes the proud, echoing the haughty eyes of verse 17. Proverbs 26:20 further develops the danger of the one who spreads strife.
basic.oneStory: This cluster of practical warnings, on debt, laziness, scheming, and God's own list of what He hates, shows that biblical wisdom reaches into the most ordinary corners of life. That same list of hated sins, false witness and shed innocent blood chief among them, was turned against the innocent Christ at His trial, so that in bearing them He might free His people from both committing and suffering under them.

context.literary:
These nineteen verses are four short poems laid end to end, and each one is tied to the next by a thread of vocabulary. The first, verses 1 to 5, ends in a rescue, a gazelle or a bird breaking free. The second, verses 6 to 11, ends in a robbery, poverty arriving "like a robber." The third, verses 12 to 15, ends in a collapse, calamity coming "suddenly." The fourth, verses 16 to 19, ends with the LORD's own list. Each unit ends on something arriving or being escaped, and the order moves from private danger to public wickedness to divine verdict.

The sleep words are the clearest thread. In verse 4 the son is told to "allow no sleep to your eyes or slumber to your eyelids," and in verse 10 the slacker enjoys "a little sleep, a little slumber." The same two nouns appear in opposite uses. Sleep is not the problem in itself. The question is whether the hour calls for rest or for action. The father tells the man in the snare to stay awake and the man in the field to get up.

The third and fourth units are joined by the body. The worthless man in verses 12 and 13 is drawn by his mouth, eyes, feet and fingers, and verses 16 to 19 run the same inventory, haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands, a heart, feet, and then two persons. The scoundrel of the portrait is a walking example of the list.

The list itself uses a numerical device, "six, indeed seven," in which the second number is the point. The same form appears in Proverbs 30:18-19 and in Job 5:19, and the climactic seventh item here is the one who stirs up discord among brothers. The whole section also interrupts the father's long speeches on adultery, which resume at 6:20 with "My son, keep your father's commandment." These verses are a pause for the practical.
context.historical:
Verses 1 to 5 reflect a credit system that ran on personal promises. A man who "struck hands" with a creditor on behalf of a neighbor was binding himself to pay if the neighbor could not, and the word translated "stranger" in verse 1 may point to a lender outside the village. The law protected the poor debtor in small ways. A borrowed cloak had to be returned by sunset, since it was his only covering, Exodus 22:26-27. Yet debt could lead to loss of land and children, as in the widow whose sons were about to be taken as slaves, 2 Kings 4:1, and the families who mortgaged their fields in Nehemiah 5:3-5. The father speaks to a young man who could lose all that through a rash promise.

The ant is a figure from a farming country. Harvester ants gather seed in the hot months, and a watcher in Israel could see them at it. Other proverbs also use the picture, "The ants are creatures of little strength, yet they store up their food in the summer," Proverbs 30:25, and "He who gathers in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son," Proverbs 10:5. Harvest was a short season, and a household that slept through it faced a hungry winter.

The portrait in verses 12 to 15 shows how a certain kind of person worked in a small town. Signals made with the eyes, feet and fingers allowed plotting without leaving anything that could be quoted in court. Proverbs 10:10 warns that the one who winks causes grief. In a society without police, trust, testimony and reputation held communities together, which is why false witness and stirring up discord were treated so seriously. The law demanded careful investigation and gave the false witness the penalty he meant for the other, Deuteronomy 19:16-19.

The worst case is Naboth. Two "scoundrels" were seated opposite him and testified falsely so that he could be stoned and his vineyard taken, 1 Kings 21:10-13. That story contains a false witness, a plot hatched in the heart and innocent blood in one episode.
context.canonical:
The chapter's separate sayings reach into other books at several points. The warning against rash security is repeated in Proverbs 11:15, 17:18 and 22:26-27, so that the book treats it as a standing danger and not a passing remark. On the other hand, suretyship is not always a fault in the Bible. Judah guaranteed Benjamin's safety to his father and later offered to take his brother's place, Genesis 43:9 and 44:32. Hebrews calls Jesus "the guarantee of a better covenant," Hebrews 7:22, using the language of a surety in a good sense.

The ant and the sluggard return in Proverbs 10:4-5, 24:30-34 and 26:13-16. The line "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest" appears word for word in Proverbs 24:33, so a reader of the book hears it twice. Paul gives the New Testament form, "If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat," 2 Thessalonians 3:10, and asks the idle to work quietly and earn their own living, verse 12.

The portrait of the worthless man draws on the Old Testament's term for the lawless. Eli's sons and the men who led a city into idolatry are given that name, 1 Samuel 2:12 and Deuteronomy 13:13, and Paul uses its Greek form, Belial, in 2 Corinthians 6:15.

The list in verses 16 to 19 is echoed by other Scripture. The feet that run to evil and are quick to shed innocent blood come almost word for word from Isaiah 59:7, which Paul quotes in his indictment of the whole human race, Romans 3:15-17. Psalm 101:5 says the LORD will not endure haughty eyes and a proud heart, and Proverbs 12:22 and 16:5 repeat that lying lips and the proud in heart are detestable to Him. Zechariah 8:16-17 gathers truthfulness, honest judgments and no plotting of evil into one command. The final item, discord among brothers, is answered in Christ's prayer that His people may be one, John 17:21.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The father wants his son to be able to handle ordinary trouble. After chapters of great themes, wisdom, the fear of the LORD and the dangers of the forbidden woman, he turns to the small matters that wreck a household without making any noise. A rash promise on a Tuesday, a long nap in the harvest and a whispered plot at the city gate are the stuff of which ruin is made.

He gives different cures for different problems. The man who has trapped himself must act at once and humbly, with no sleep until he is free. The man who is drifting needs a teacher, and he is sent to the ant. The son who is tempted to scheme sees what the scheming man looks like from outside, with a perverse mouth, winking eyes and gestures that hide his purpose, and is told how it ends. Then the father steps back and names what God hates, so that the son knows what to avoid.

The list does something the earlier stories could not. It teaches the son to see his own heart. A young man may not think of himself as a murderer or a false witness, but he may recognize a proud look or a quick word in himself. Put as a list, sins that look small are shown to sit in the same family as sins that look large.

Finally, the father wants the son to take God's feelings seriously. These are not social conventions but the things the LORD hates, and the son is meant to love what He loves. The list gives a moral compass by pointing to the grief of the God he serves.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first unit is a response to a specific situation, "if you have put up security." The advice is addressed to someone already caught, and it is practical and urgent. The warning against becoming a guarantor is a general principle in Proverbs, but the Bible also praises costly guarantees made with open eyes, Genesis 43:9 and Hebrews 7:22, so the verses are not a ban on every act of financial help. They teach caution about promises that can ruin a household.

The ant is a lesson, not a law of nature or a command to work without rest. Rest is part of the same Bible, for God gives sleep to His beloved, Psalm 127:2, and "The sleep of the worker is sweet," Ecclesiastes 5:12. The charge is aimed at the person who stays in bed in the season when work is needed. Nor should the picture of poverty arriving like a robber be applied to every poor person. Proverbs says elsewhere that food in the fields of the poor can be swept away "without justice," Proverbs 13:23. The verses describe one cause of poverty and should not be used to judge another.

The list of seven is a description of what God hates and an implied command to avoid it. The six-seven pattern is a literary form meaning the list is complete enough to be useful, and not a claim that God hates exactly seven things. Other passages add lying lips, dishonest scales and the proud, Proverbs 11:1, 12:22 and 16:5.

Application falls in two steps. First, treat the sins in the list as warnings for oneself before they are accusations against others. Second, remember that the same Bible tells of One who was betrayed by this very list and who forgave. Believers are called to hate evil, Psalm 97:10, and also to love enemies, Matthew 5:44.

debates.question: Does the warning against pledging security, verses 1 to 5, forbid all financial guarantees or cosigning?

views.label: A blanket warning against ever guaranteeing another's debt
views.case: The urgency of the language, free yourself like a gazelle from a hunter, suggests the practice itself is inherently dangerous and to be avoided.

views.label: A warning against reckless, ill considered pledges specifically
views.case: The passage targets rash, trapped commitments, having struck hands with a stranger, verse 1, rather than every conceivable financial guarantee; wisdom elsewhere assumes some financial cooperation between neighbors is normal, so the concern is imprudent entanglement, not cooperative generosity as such.

debates.bearing: Read alongside the rest of Proverbs, which commends generosity and neighborly help, the wiser reading treats this as a warning against reckless, poorly considered financial entanglement, especially with strangers, rather than a blanket prohibition on ever helping to guarantee a trustworthy neighbor's need.

debates.question: Is poverty in verse 11 always the result of idleness?

views.label: Poverty follows idleness as a reliable rule
views.case: The verse says poverty will come on the sleeper like a robber, and Proverbs 10:4 says idle hands make one poor. On this reading the book teaches that diligence is the ordinary road to enough and laziness the ordinary road to want.

views.label: The proverb states one cause among several
views.case: Proverbs 13:23 says the food of the poor is swept away 'without justice,' and the book elsewhere tells readers not to exploit the poor. On this reading verse 11 addresses a person who could work and will not, and does not describe every poor person.

debates.bearing: The book itself holds both facts. Idleness leads to want, and injustice also creates it. The verses are an appeal to the sluggard and not a verdict on the poor, so they should be used to rouse the person who is drifting and never to blame the person who is crushed.

debates.question: Does God hate sinners or only sin, in verses 16 to 19?

views.label: God hates sinful acts and attitudes, not persons
views.case: The list names eyes, a tongue, hands, a heart, feet and a witness, which are the instruments of sin, and the Bible says God loved the world and desires that no one perish, John 3:16 and 2 Peter 3:9. On this reading the hatred is aimed at the evil and the harm it does.

views.label: God's hatred reaches the persons who practice evil
views.case: Some verses speak of God's hatred of people, 'You hate all workers of iniquity,' Psalm 5:5, and 'His soul hates the lover of violence,' Psalm 11:5. Verse 19 also names persons, the false witness and the one who sows discord, as detestable.

views.label: A holy opposition to evil that sits alongside love
views.case: A third view sees these as two sides of one holy character. God's wrath and His patience are both real, and the Bible does not always draw the line between the sinner and the sin because the sinner is bound up in what he does until he repents.

debates.bearing: The text names God's reaction in strong terms and should not be softened, because the LORD is not neutral about pride, lies, violence and division. But the surrounding Scripture shows a God who gives time to turn and who has made a way for the guilty to be forgiven, so that the hatred of evil never cancels His offer of mercy.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 uses a verb that means to give a pledge or stand as a guarantor, arab, and its relative appears in Genesis 43:9, where Judah says he will guarantee Benjamin's safety, and in Genesis 44:32. The same word is used in Isaiah 38:14, where the sick king prays, "O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security." So the word is not only a financial term. It carries the sense of taking on another's risk, and Proverbs warns against taking on a risk that one cannot carry. The gesture of "striking hands" is a physical sign of a deal, as in Proverbs 17:18, and the father says it can become a trap, since the very mouth that made the promise catches the speaker, verse 2.

In verse 6 the slacker is atsel, a word found almost only in Proverbs, and the ant, namlah, is set before him as a teacher. The command is to observe and "become wise," so the lesson is learned by looking, as other proverbs teach by pointing to creatures. In verse 10 the three phrases, "a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands," use the same Hebrew words for sleep and slumber that were forbidden in verse 4. The smallness of each word is the point, since it shows how a long loss is built from short moments.

Verse 12 calls the man beliyya'al, a word the BSB translates "worthless person." Its derivation is debated. The common view takes it as "without worth," and the term is used of men who corrupt others, as in the sons of Eli, 1 Samuel 2:12, and the two witnesses against Naboth, 1 Kings 21:10. The man "walks with a perverse mouth," and the phrase for a perverse mouth is the one the father used in Proverbs 4:24 when he told his son to put it away. His eyes, feet and fingers carry messages without words. The verb in verse 14 for "sows discord" is a verb of sending, so he keeps sending strife out like seed.

Verse 15 says calamity will come "suddenly," a word that also stands in Proverbs 3:25, where the son is told not to fear "sudden danger." The difference lies in the person. The one who walks with wisdom is told not to fear it, and the one who sows discord is told it is coming for him. The Hebrew for "beyond recovery" is literally "without healing," and the word for healing here is the one used in Proverbs 4:22 of the health that the father's words give. The one who rejects wisdom reaches a state in which healing is no longer available. Proverbs 29:1 uses the same phrase of the stiff-necked.

In verse 16 the word for "detestable" is toebah, the strong word used for idolatry and dishonest scales. The Hebrew says that these seven are detestable to His "soul," nefesh, which makes the hatred a matter of God's inmost being. Psalm 11:5 uses the same idea when it says His soul hates the lover of violence. And in verse 19 the false witness is one who "breathes out lies," a picture of lying as an exhalation that comes as naturally as breath.

typology.type: The false witness and the shedder of innocent blood, Proverbs 6:17-19
typology.fulfillment: Three of the items on the list met in the trial of Jesus. Many 'bore false witness against Jesus, but their testimony was inconsistent,' Mark 14:56, the chief priests and elders conspired to arrest Him covertly and kill Him, Matthew 26:3-4, and Judas said, 'I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,' Matthew 27:4. The proverb describes what God hates, and in the passion the hated things are done to His Son. The same pattern appeared in Naboth's case, 1 Kings 21:10-13. The type falls short because Naboth was only a righteous man wronged, while Jesus was wronged by the list and then bore its guilt on behalf of those who did it, Isaiah 53:5.

typology.type: The guarantor who takes on another's debt, Proverbs 6:1-5
typology.fulfillment: The proverb warns against becoming responsible for what one cannot pay. Judah offered himself as security for Benjamin and later asked to stay as a slave in his place, Genesis 43:9 and 44:32. Hebrews applies the same language to Christ, 'Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant,' Hebrews 7:22, and Paul says He became poor for our sake, 2 Corinthians 8:9. The difference is complete. The human guarantor in the proverb is told to escape because he cannot pay. Christ guaranteed a debt He could pay and did, so the type falls short at the point where the proverb is wise and the gospel is greater.

typology.type: The ant that works without a commander, Proverbs 6:6-8
typology.fulfillment: The ant is a sign of work done in the proper season without outside pressure. Jesus describes His own mission in similar terms, 'While it is daytime, we must do the works of Him who sent Me. Night is coming, when no one can work,' John 9:4. Paul asks believers to work with their hands so as to need no one's help and to have something to share, Ephesians 4:28. The proverb is a lesson in diligence and not a prediction of Christ, so the link is by pattern. The type is limited, because the ant works for its own store, while Christ worked for those who could not work their way out of their debt.

typology.type: The sower of discord against the Peacemaker, Proverbs 6:14, 19
typology.fulfillment: The man who 'continually sows discord' and the one who stirs up trouble among brothers is the opposite of the One Paul describes, 'He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility,' Ephesians 2:14. Jesus blesses the peacemakers as sons of God, Matthew 5:9, and prays that all His people may be one, John 17:21. The contrast does not claim that the proverb predicts Christ. It shows that the seventh and most serious item on the list is the very thing His work undoes, and the type falls short only in that Christ makes the peace at the cost of His own body.

study.christ:
The way into Christ from this passage is not through a single image but through the list. Verses 16 to 19 name what the LORD hates, and the Gospels show those very things converging on His Son. Proud men sought to destroy Him, and false witnesses were brought forward, though "their testimony was inconsistent," Mark 14:56. A heart "that devises wicked schemes" is the plot of the chief priests and elders, who "conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him," Matthew 26:3-4. Feet "that run swiftly to evil" are the feet of men who came out with swords and clubs. Hands that shed innocent blood are named by Judas, who said, "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood," Matthew 27:4. The list describes in advance, in general terms, the crime that was committed against Jesus.

Then the Cross reveals what stands behind it. The seven things are detestable to God, yet God gave His Son into the hands of sinful men, Acts 2:23. That is not a contradiction. The Son bore what the list describes. Isaiah says He was pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, Isaiah 53:5. The sins that the proverb names as hated are the ones the Lamb took away.

Look next at the guarantor of verses 1 to 5. The father tells the man who has stood surety for another to get free as quickly as he can, because he cannot cover the debt. Scripture also shows a guarantee that does not fail. Judah's offer to stay in his brother's place, Genesis 44:32, prepares for a greater Judah, and Hebrews calls Jesus "the guarantee of a better covenant," Hebrews 7:22. King Hezekiah prays in his illness, "be my security," Isaiah 38:14. Christ is the One who answers that prayer. He took on a debt that was not His and could pay it, and He did so humbly, being "obedient to death," Philippians 2:8.

Next, the sower of discord. The seventh item is the thing He came to reverse. He "made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility," Ephesians 2:14, and He called the peacemakers sons of God, Matthew 5:9. The one who divides brothers works against the prayer of Jesus that His people may be one, John 17:21.

Finally, the ant and the slacker point to the One who worked while it was day, John 9:4, and who rose early to pray, Mark 1:35. Jesus Himself taught diligence in the parables of the talents, Matthew 25:14-30.

Some caution is needed. The chapter does not predict Jesus' trial, and the typological links should be held as patterns the New Testament makes visible and not as a code in the proverb. What the passage gives is a clear description of human wickedness and God's reaction to it. The Gospels show that this wickedness did its worst to Christ, and that He answered with forgiveness, "Father, forgive them," Luke 23:34.
study.god:
The most striking thing in the passage is that it speaks of the LORD's emotions. "There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are detestable to Him," verse 16. The Hebrew says they are detestable to His soul. This is not a cold judge reading a statute. It is a God who is personally involved in the harm done to His creatures, and whose displeasure is as real as His delight. Proverbs 12:22 sets the two sides together, "Lying lips are detestable to the LORD, but those who deal faithfully are His delight." The LORD feels about truthfulness and falsehood, and a worshipper is meant to learn to feel as He does.

The seven items are all about harm to other people. A proud look looks down on others. A lying tongue and a false witness damage trust and justice. Hands that shed innocent blood destroy life. A scheming heart and feet that rush to evil plan and carry out harm. The one who sows discord among brothers breaks the community God has made. The list shows that God's holiness is not narrowly religious. It is concerned with how people treat one another, and His anger is aimed at the things that crush His image bearers.

Another thing the passage shows is God's patience in practical matters. The man caught in a promise is told to go and humble himself and try to get out. The slacker is asked, "How long will you lie there?" and "When will you get up?" verse 9. These are the questions of a teacher and not of an executioner. The Lord who hates the proud is also the one who delivers from the snare of the fowler, Psalm 91:3, and the writer of Psalm 124 can say, "We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler," Psalm 124:7. The gazelle and the bird of verse 5 are pictures of rescue, and Scripture says that God is the One who rescues.

The passage also shows God's justice with its timing. "Calamity will come upon him suddenly; in an instant he will be shattered beyond recovery," verse 15. The suddenness is the end of a long slow plotting, but it is not a delayed accident. It is the moral order the LORD made, and Proverbs 29:1 says the same of the stiff-necked. God is slow to anger and does not leave guilt unanswered.

For worship, the chapter asks for an honest heart. We can sing of God's love only if we also learn what He hates and ask Him to search us, Psalm 139:23-24. We can thank Him that the sins on this list are not beyond His mercy, and that He gives us diligence and peace in their place. A believer who hates what God hates and loves what He loves has begun to be wise.

crossReferences.note: Judah says he guaranteed the boy's safety to his father and asks to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place. This is the Bible's best picture of a guarantee made with open eyes. It shows that Proverbs 6:1-5 does not condemn self sacrifice for another. It warns against pledges made without counting the cost.

Warns against giving pledges, and asks why a man's bed should be taken from under him if he cannot pay. It develops the picture of ruin in 6:1-5 and gives the practical stakes. A household could lose its basic comfort, and the proverb treats such security as a danger to avoid.

Repeats verses 10 and 11 word for word, a little sleep, a little slumber and poverty like a robber. The repetition shows how the book treats idleness as a settled danger, and the context in chapter 24 adds the picture of a neglected field that the sluggard's neglect has overgrown.

Says that ants are creatures of little strength yet they store up their food in summer. It supports the lesson of verses 6 to 8 by making the ant an example of wisdom for the weak. The father in chapter 6 uses the ant to rebuke the strong who will not move.

Says that the feet of the wicked run to evil and are swift to shed innocent blood, with sinful thoughts. It is close to verses 17 and 18, and shows the prophet drawing on the same pattern of wickedness. Isaiah applies it to Israel's rulers and people as a charge of covenant breach.

Paul quotes Isaiah's description of feet swift to shed blood in his case that all people are under sin. The proverb's list of what God hates is thereby read as a mirror held to everyone. The text moves from warning against particular offenders to showing that no one is outside it.

Two scoundrels testify falsely against Naboth so that he can be stoned and his vineyard seized. It is a case study of verses 12 to 19, with a false witness, a heart that devises schemes and innocent blood, all in one account. It shows that the list describes real events in Israel's history.

Lays down that a proven false witness must receive the penalty he meant for the accused. It gives the legal background to verse 19. The proverb names the false witness among the things God hates, and the law shows the community's attempt to deal with it.

Calls Jesus the guarantee of a better covenant, using the language of surety in a good sense. Where Proverbs warns against pledging for what one cannot pay, Hebrews says Christ pledged what He could pay. The word helps a reader see the warning and the gospel without confusing them.

Says the LORD tests the righteous and the wicked and that His soul hates the lover of violence. It supports the way Proverbs 6:16 speaks of God's soul and shows that the hatred named in the list is a settled part of His character. The context shows He also upholds the righteous.

Says that Christ is our peace, has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility. It answers the seventh item in verse 19. Where one person stirs up discord among brothers, Christ creates one new people through the cross, and the New Testament sets His work beside the proverb's warning.

Judas says he has sinned by betraying innocent blood. The phrase picks up the third item on the list, hands that shed innocent blood, and places it at the trial of Jesus. It shows how fully the proverb's description of hated things is realized in the events surrounding the Cross.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a world where work is a gift. Adam was put in the garden to work it and keep it, Genesis 2:15, and the pull of the passage's ant comes from that original design. After the fall work becomes toil, Genesis 3:17-19, and laziness and greed are two ways of living badly under that curse. The warnings in these verses speak into the ordinary life of fallen people, the life of debts, harvests and market days where wisdom is needed more than heroics.

The list of seven also reads like a summary of what the story goes wrong with. Pride is the sin of the serpent's offer and of Babel, and lying begins with "Did God really say?" Genesis 3:1. Innocent blood is the first cry from the ground in Genesis 4:10, and discord among brothers starts with Cain and Abel. The scheming heart, the eager feet and the false witness fill the later history of Israel, as in the story of Naboth. In a few lines the father summarizes the trouble the whole Bible is trying to undo.

The center of the story takes the list upon itself. At the trial of Jesus every item on the list is present. Pride, lies, innocent blood, plotting, haste to evil and discord all gather against Him, and He does not return any of it. He was the guarantee of a better covenant, Hebrews 7:22, who took the debt of others on Himself, and He made peace between brothers by His death, Ephesians 2:14-16. The sins God hates are the very sins He bore, and His rising declares that they have been dealt with.

The new creation is where the list is finally empty. The book of Revelation says that nothing unclean and no one who practices falsehood will enter the city, Revelation 21:27, and that there will be no more curse, Revelation 22:3. Work then will be service without toil, since His servants will serve Him, Revelation 22:3. The people who have been forgiven and changed are brothers and sisters who live together in unity. The proverb's wish for a life without pride, falsehood, violence and division comes true in the people God makes, and the One who hated those things is among them, wiping away every tear.

quiz.q: What urgent action does verse 3 to 5 counsel for someone who has recklessly pledged security for another?

options.text: Go humbly and urgently to free yourself from the pledge without delay.
options.note: The passage's language, allow no sleep, free yourself like a gazelle, stresses urgency and humility.

options.text: Ignore it, since such pledges carry no real risk.
options.note: The passage treats this as a serious, urgent trap, not something to ignore.

options.text: Wait patiently for the debt to resolve itself over time.
options.note: The text calls for immediate, active effort, not passive waiting.

options.text: Take legal action against the neighbor immediately.
options.note: The passage instead counsels humbling oneself and pleading with the neighbor directly, not adversarial legal action.

quiz.q: What lesson does the ant teach the sluggard, verses 6 to 8?

options.text: Diligent work does not require external supervision to get done.
options.note: Verse 7 stresses the ant works without commander, overseer, or ruler.

options.text: Hard work is unnecessary if you are naturally gifted.
options.note: The passage's whole point is the necessity and value of diligent effort.

options.text: Rest is always wrong and should be entirely avoided.
options.note: The rebuke targets excessive, self ruining laziness, not rest as such.

options.text: Community leadership is the only path to productivity.
options.note: The passage's point is nearly the opposite, the ant is productive precisely without any leader directing it.

quiz.q: How does the passage describe the 'worthless person' in verses 12 to 15?

options.text: A schemer who sows discord through deceptive body language and faces sudden, irrecoverable ruin.
options.note: This matches the description exactly, winking, pointing, plotting evil, and sudden calamity.

options.text: Someone who is simply poor and unfortunate.
options.note: The passage's concern is moral character and scheming, not poverty.

options.text: A respected elder whose counsel is trusted.
options.note: The passage portrays the opposite, a deceitful troublemaker, not a trusted elder.

options.text: A careless but harmless gossip.
options.note: This understates the passage's description of active, deceitful scheming toward evil, not mere careless talk.

quiz.q: According to verses 16 to 19, which of the following is among the things the LORD hates?

options.text: A false witness who gives false testimony and one who stirs up discord among brothers.
options.note: Both appear explicitly in the closing list, verse 19.

options.text: Honest confession of sin.
options.note: Honest confession is commended throughout Scripture, the opposite of what this list condemns.

options.text: Careful and diligent labor.
options.note: Diligent labor is commended earlier in this very passage through the example of the ant, not condemned.

options.text: Humility before God and others.
options.note: Humility is the opposite of the haughty eyes this list actually condemns; it is commended, not hated, throughout Proverbs.

quiz.q: How does the list of things the LORD hates connect to the trial of Jesus?

options.text: False witnesses and hands eager to shed innocent blood, both named as detestable, converged against Jesus at His trial.
options.note: Matthew 26:59-60 records false witnesses sought against Jesus, matching the sins this list names.

options.text: It has no connection to the Gospel accounts at all.
options.note: The Gospel trial narratives directly display the very sins this list condemns.

options.text: It shows that Jesus Himself committed these sins.
options.note: The Gospels present Jesus as entirely innocent, the victim of these sins, not their perpetrator.

options.text: It only applies to Old Testament legal disputes, with no New Testament relevance.
options.note: This understates the direct connection the Gospel writers draw between false testimony against Jesus and exactly this kind of sin.

questions: The passage urges urgent, humble action to escape a reckless financial entanglement. Is there a commitment or debt you have been avoiding dealing with, hoping it will resolve on its own?
The ant works diligently without any supervisor watching. Where in your life are you tempted to coast, doing your best work only when someone is checking on you?

The worthless schemer plots evil through subtle body language, winking, pointing, before sudden ruin. Are there small, seemingly minor ways you manipulate or mislead others that could be quietly building toward real harm?
Of the seven things the LORD hates, which one do you most need to examine in your own heart this week, pride, lying, violence, scheming, eagerness for evil, false testimony, or stirring up discord?

Christ bore the very sins this passage names, false witness and shed innocent blood, at His own trial. How does knowing He absorbed these exact sins change how you view both your own guilt and those who have wronged you?

translationNotes.note: Press your plea can also be rendered hasten, or urge, stressing the urgency of resolving a reckless pledge without delay.
The pattern 'six things, seven' is a common device in Hebrew poetry for a complete or representative list, not a claim that God hates only these seven things and nothing more.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture toolkit for Proverbs 6:1-19. Poetic line breaks within verses 17 to 19 in the source were rendered as flowing prose.
